faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Common questions about rubber component design, manufacturing, and quality assurance.

q1.question: What is the typical lead time for custom rubber parts?
q1.answer: Standard lead times range from 2-4 weeks for existing tooling, and 4-6 weeks for new tooling development. Prototype parts can often be delivered within 1-2 weeks using rapid tooling methods.

q2.question: How do I choose the right rubber material for my application?
q2.answer: Material selection depends on temperature range, chemical exposure, mechanical requirements, and application standards and operating conditions. Our material selection guide provides detailed comparison data, or contact our engineering team for recommendations.

q3.question: What tolerance levels can you achieve?
q3.answer: We routinely achieve ISO 3302 Class M1 tolerances (±0.05mm for small parts). Tighter tolerances are possible with specialized tooling and process control - consult our engineering team for feasibility.

q4.question: Do you provide PPAP documentation?
q4.answer: Yes, we provide full PPAP documentation including Level 3 submissions with all supporting data. Our quality management system is IATF 16949 certified, ensuring automotive-grade documentation standards.

q5.question: Can you work with customer-supplied materials?
q5.answer: Yes, we can process customer-supplied materials or source specific grades as required. All materials undergo incoming inspection and verification before use in production.

hero.title: The RubberQ Standard
hero.subtitle: Our two-stage mixing process — run on a single, dedicated A-mixing line designed with our Japanese formulation partners — is the backbone of our quality promise. By separating masterbatching from final compounding, we achieve superior batch-to-batch consistency across years of production for critical EV, semiconductor, and Tier 2 automotive applications.

singleLineCallout.title: Single-Line Mixing Control
singleLineCallout.body: RubberQ schedules compound families by contamination risk, runs SOP-based cleaning between batch families, and keeps A-mixing records tied to the batch. This supports high-purity and long-term repeatability needs without exposing customer-specific recipes.

abMixing.title: A-Mixing, B-Mixing, and Batch Release Control
abMixing.intro: The process flow separates masterbatch preparation from final cure-system addition. This reduces formulation drift, improves traceability, and gives the lab a defined release gate before molding.

stages.title: Masterbatch foundation
stages.body: Base polymer, filler, oil, and reinforcement materials are weighed, barcode-checked, mixed, sheeted, cooled, and screened for foreign matter before release.

stages.title: Intermediate material check
stages.body: A-compound can be checked for dispersion, specific gravity, and Mooney viscosity before it moves to final mixing.

stages.title: Cure-system addition
stages.body: Accelerators and cure-system ingredients are added later under process instruction, then the compound is matured, cut, stored, and prepared for molding.

stages.title: Lab gate before molding
stages.body: Rheometer curve, hardness, tensile strength, elongation, and drawing-specific checks confirm the batch is suitable for production.
